name: Negative (apophatic) theology and the unknowability of God
plain_explanation: Following the pseudo-Dionysius, John the Scot holds that God's essence is unknowable, even to angels, and in a sense even to Himself, since 'He is not a what.' Affirmative statements about God (that He is truth, goodness, essence) are only symbolically true, because every ordinary predicate has an opposite, while God has none.
precise_definition: The doctrine that God cannot be positively defined or comprehended by any finite intellect, so that all cataphatic (affirmative) statements about the divine nature must be understood symbolically rather than literally, while the more fundamental theological method is apophatic (negative), proceeding by denial.
why_it_mattered: It shaped John's account of how creatures relate to and differ from God (always 'by a negation'), and transmitted an influential strand of Neoplatonic mysticism into medieval Christian philosophy via his translation of the pseudo-Dionysius.
historical_origin: Derived directly from the pseudo-Dionysius, itself rooted in Neoplatonic (probably Proclean) philosophy.
examples: "God does not know Himself, what He is, because He is not a what; in a certain respect He is incomprehensible to Himself and to every intellect."
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes a parallel with F. H. Bradley's view that no truth is quite true, though the best available truth is not intellectually correctable.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Bears on how theology can speak of God at all.
